# The Coronary Slow Flow Phenomenon: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and Definition

The coronary slow flow phenomenon (CSFP) is an angiographic entity characterized by delayed distal opacification of the epicardial coronary arteries in the absence of significant obstructive disease. It was first described by Tambe, Demany, Zimmerman, and Mascarenhas in 1972 in the American Heart Journal as a new angiographic finding in patients with angina and slow flow velocity of dye in the coronary arteries. It is now understood as an angiographic finding characterized by delayed distal vessel opacification in the absence of significant epicardial coronary disease. Some authors regard it as a distinct microvascular disorder, and it has variously been termed coronary slow flow syndrome or cardiac "syndrome Y" [2,3].

Quantification became more objective with the introduction of the corrected TIMI frame count (CTFC). Although the TIMI flow grade is a valuable and widely used qualitative measure, it is limited by its subjective and categorical nature; Gibson and colleagues counted the number of cineframes needed for dye to reach standardized distal landmarks to objectively assess coronary blood flow as a continuous variable, and the method was shown to be reproducible. In normal arteries the left anterior descending coronary artery frame count was approximately 1.7 times longer than the mean of the right coronary and circumflex counts, a difference corrected by dividing the LAD count by 1.7. A CTFC above 27 frames in at least one of the three major vessels is commonly used to define CSFP.

## Epidemiology and Risk Factors

CSFP is not a rare curiosity. It has an incidence of 1–5% in patients undergoing coronary angiography and has been most frequently found in young men who are smokers with metabolic syndrome. In a large angiographic series, CSFP was identified in 96 (5.5%) of subjects referred for angiography, and those affected were more obese and had lower high-density lipoprotein levels, with higher total cholesterol and low-density lipoprotein. Other cohorts have reinforced the association with conventional risk factors: there was a significantly higher prevalence of hypertension, dyslipidemia, and tobacco use in CSFP patients compared with controls, and on multivariable analysis hypertension, dyslipidemia, smoking, and tobacco chewing were independently associated with CSFP. Patients also more often present with rest pain requiring urgent admission, usually to a coronary care unit.

## Pathophysiology

Several overlapping mechanisms have been proposed. Microvascular dysfunction has been central since the first descriptions: small vessel dysfunction has typically been implicated in the pathogenesis of CSFP, with investigators reporting fibromuscular hyperplasia, medial hypertrophy, myointimal proliferation, and endothelial edema, thickening, and degeneration in the coronary microvessels. Beltrame and colleagues indicated that CSFP was associated with a chronically elevated resting coronary microvascular tone characterized by low coronary sinus oxygen saturation and blunted responses to endothelial stimuli.

Endothelial dysfunction is strongly implicated. In one study, endothelin-1 and nitric oxide concentrations were assessed before and at peak exercise in slow coronary flow patients compared with healthy controls, in whom the mean TIMI frame count was markedly elevated, supporting impaired endothelial vasoregulation. Systemic inflammation is also relevant: an increased high-sensitivity C-reactive protein level suggests that inflammation may be associated with, or at least contribute to, the pathogenesis of slow coronary flow and may be an early marker of impaired coronary blood flow. Altered platelet biology has been observed as well, with mean platelet volume increased in patients with slow coronary flow, particularly in those presenting with unstable angina, suggesting altered platelet reactivity that may require effective antiplatelet therapy.

Importantly, whether CSFP equates to microvascular dysfunction has been questioned. Although guidelines suggest CTFC >27 can diagnose microvascular dysfunction, studies using simultaneous coronary pressure and flow velocity have found only weak correlations, with CTFC showing a weak negative correlation with basal peak velocity and a weak positive correlation with basal microvascular resistance.

## Clinical Presentation and Prognosis

Clinically, CSFP can present as angina pectoris, acute coronary syndrome, and sudden cardiac death. Recurrent symptoms are common and burdensome: over 80% of patients experience recurrent chest pain, resulting in considerable impairment in quality of life. Although overall mortality is low, electrical instability is a recognized concern. A reported case of CSFP normalized with intracoronary adenosine but featured multiple episodes of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia and increased QTc dispersion, responding well to oral dipyridamole with resolution of symptoms at three months.

## Management

There is no established standard therapy. Calcium channel blockers are among the best studied. A study of the T-channel blocker mibefradil reduced the number of vessels exhibiting TIMI-2 flow, improved TIMI frame count in affected vessels, and—compared with placebo—significantly reduced total angina frequency by 56% and prolonged angina episodes by 74%. However, mibefradil was withdrawn from general therapeutic availability owing to cytochrome P450 3A4 inhibition and resultant drug interactions. In a randomized trial, sustained-release diltiazem improved coronary blood flow and alleviated angina, whereas these parameters remained unchanged in the control group.

Microvascular vasodilators have shown angiographic benefit. Dipyridamole, which has dilatory properties on coronary microvessels, proved to be an effective treatment in most patients with slow coronary artery flow. Agents targeting endothelial function also appear promising. After nebivolol therapy, chest pain relief was detected in 90% of patients, and systolic and diastolic blood pressure and high-sensitivity CRP were significantly reduced. Statins may exert pleiotropic benefit: atorvastatin significantly decreased total cholesterol, triglycerides, LDL-C, hs-CRP, endothelin-1 and IL-6 while increasing nitric oxide, with significant improvement in CTFC and endothelial progenitor cell function, suggesting that it can treat CSF by suppressing inflammation and improving endothelial function.

## Conclusion

More than five decades after its description, CSFP remains incompletely understood. Although well known to interventional cardiologists for approximately four decades, the pathogenic mechanisms remain unclear. The convergence of microvascular, endothelial, inflammatory, and prothrombotic abnormalities suggests CSFP is a systemic vascular disorder rather than a benign curiosity. Larger randomized trials with clinical endpoints are needed to establish evidence-based therapy.
